#6732. The Rise and Rise of Adéla

It’s 9 p.m. on a Tuesday and I’m four floors underground, at a sweaty central London club. Surrounding me are roughly 2,000 Gen-Zers in pink wigs and fishnets chanting—between surreptitious vape puffs—the lyrics to a then unreleased song. “I got boys, like a vending machine,” voices boom around me as Adéla, her lithe ballet dancer’s figure clad in a denim-and-rhinestone bralette and hot pants, flips her hair Baywatch-style and kicks her leg so far it flies all the way back over her head. (They’re the kind of moves that, if I attempted them, paramedics would have to be called.) There’s peak-Britney choreo for the bangers, peak-Xtina vocals on the ballads, cheeky foul-mouthed banter in between—she commands the stage like a veteran.

Dilara Findikoglu silk corset jacket and skirt. Heavenly London zirconia and velvet choker.

Twelve hours later, the Slovakian pop renegade bounces around a light-filled rehearsal room at the English National Ballet School, spinning like a whirling dervish in a black Chanel gown for her British Vogue shoot, still in the thick of an August heatwave. If Adéla is tired, she doesn’t let on. “I think because I’m 22… that helps,” she says with a mischievous grin as we sit down afterwards, running her talon-like acrylic nails through her signature pink locks. (She’s recently dyed her hair a deeper, dirtier magenta in place of her previous pastel hue: “My fans say I gain more power the pinker my hair gets.”) Her gaze falls on the ballet barres and mirrored walls, and she pauses: Adéla has history here, having moved from Bratislava to study dance in these exact rooms as a 15-year-old. “I met one of my best friends, Luca, here—he was my first fan,” she recalls. “He was like, ‘I feel like you could be a pop star.’ So I have fond memories of this place.”

Adéla’s journey to becoming this year’s most-buzzed-about music breakout has been uncommonly well-documented. Originally cast in 2023 as a contestant for the K-pop reality show that formed Katseye, she was booted out early partly because—despite becoming a fan favorite in Netflix’s subsequent docuseries—the judges sensed she was destined for solo stardom. She seized upon the exposure, independently releasing her early songs and music videos and building a cult following among internet pop savants, then signing with Capitol Records in 2025 and releasing her debut EP, The Provocateur, last summer to rave reviews. (The eye-popping album artwork features Adéla pulling up her dress and urinating in the street; you can understand why she was never built for the clean-cut confines of a manufactured pop group.)

Marc Jacobs slip dress, T-shirt, and tights. Ebay pre-loved boots. Completedworks necklace.

And when I meet her, Adéla is on the precipice of her biggest leap yet: just over a week later, she’s releasing her debut album, Prima, and its third single, “Ain’t in LA,” is surging up the charts globally. The song, which recalls the world-dominating hits of Miley Cyrus’s Bangerz era, is a celebration of the cool girls in “unknown cities” around the world—“It’s all a lie, the baddest bitches ain’t in LA,” she sings on the euphoric chorus—and the video features Adéla running through the streets of Bratislava, posing with breakdancing kids in Slovak folk costumes, and rolling around with her mom and younger sister at home. (Both are in town for the concert and sit to watch her pose for the shoot, visibly beaming with pride.) The most recent single, “Nicole Kidman,” is also a viral sensation, with a video referencing some of the actor’s most iconic roles (“Moulin Rouge, my corset is so tight”) and her internet-favorite AMC adt; Kidman herself is a fan, calling Adéla “so talented.”

Her label didn’t think “Ain’t in LA” should be a single and she had to push for it, she says. “There are so many forces at play that pull you a thousand different directions when you’re an artist—and they want what’s best for you. It’s not like they’re evil, but they might pull you away from something really great.” Her assessment of why they might not have understood it initially is equally frank: “I think the people in my label didn’t necessarily resonate with it because they’re LA rich kids. No shade, but they are. And that’s what a lot of the music industry is.”

Chanel leather dress, fringed viscose skirt, and laminated leather shoes.

It’s that candor—and wry sense of humor—that has endeared her to her rapidly growing fanbase: nearly six million across Instagram and TikTok (and counting). She’s still learning to navigate the intensity of that fame, especially as some fans have pushed back about her switching up her sound from the gnarly electroclash of her EP to the more polished pop of Prima: “Going on socials and seeing what everybody’s saying… I guess I’m going to learn how to deal with that.” She visibly steels herself. “It’s definitely tough.”

That meteoric rise has already turned her into a fashion-world darling: working with creative director Chris Horan—Charli xcx’s longtime stylist and a key architect of the Brat-osphere—she’s already scored a Mac Cosmetics campaign, a front-row seat at Saint Laurent’s Paris Fashion Week show, and a killer Marc Jacobs look at the CFDA Awards, complete with skyscraper platforms. “I had to hold onto somebody [to walk in them],” she says, with a deep laugh. “They kept passing me to each other like I was a baby the entire event. But I’ll do anything for a fashion moment.”

Adéla is a devoted scholar of pop stardom and lights up when I mention the crowd the previous night cosplaying as her in their wigs and leg warmers. (The most popular look? Hot-pink T-shirts reading: “The baddest bitches are in London.”) “That’s definitely a thing that I think every good pop star has,” she says. “When I was nine, I used to wear a half-down ponytail every day of my life because of Ariana Grande.” It feels like that’s who Adéla is doing it all for: not the fans online, not entirely for herself today, but for that young girl growing up in Bratislava with posters of Ariana and Miley and Beyoncé on her wall. “I wanted to make an album that I knew if I listened to it when I was nine, 10, 11, I would’ve been like, ‘This is sick.’”

Hair, Masaki Kameda; makeup, Bea Sweet. Nails: Ella Vivii. With thanks to the English National Ballet School.

#6731. Everything We Know About The Batman: Part II Thanks to… Heidi Klum?

If you’d told me even a month ago we’d get significant spoilers for The Batman: Part II, the next Robert Pattinson-led Batman movie, in a photo Heidi Klum posted for her annual Halloween costume, I would find that both weirdly specific and entirely unbelievable.

And yet, that looks to be exactly what happened this past weekend when prosthetics supplier The Makeup Armoury posted BTS photos of the work prosthetics expert Mike Marino (who also worked to transform Colin Farrell into The Penguin for the first film and subsequent HBO Max series) was doing for Klum. If you’ve somehow been off-grid for the last few years, you may have missed that the famed supermodel takes Halloween incredibly seriously, frequently donning costumes with extensive makeup and designs that make her unrecognizable. This year was no exception, but it might have gone largely unnoticed had that photo not accidentally revealed clues about the upcoming superhero sequel, which is currently in production with an expected release date of February 18th, 2028.

In the photo, Marino, who provided a helping, ahem, hand in Klum’s costume together for the year, had a number of molds lingering in the background, which have seemingly confirmed that Brian Tyree Henry will play Two-Face, Sebastian Stan will play Victor Zsasz, and that Part II will feature the famed Court of Owls.

Henry’s mold appears to show the Atlanta actor with a disfigured face that mimics the iconic villain. Some, including me, in this very outlet, have, speculated that he might be playing either Dent or Detective Harvey Bullock, a hardened Gotham City cop who frequently works alongside Jim Gordon. But this seems to confirm it. Considering writer-director Matt Reeves has cited Jeph Loeb and Tim Sale’s The Long Halloween as an influence on his version of the Caped Crusader, it’s not ultimately a huge surprise, but perhaps a slight disappointment considering Reeves had stated his intention to move the sequel into uncharted territory by featuring a villain that had “never really been done in a film before.”

Which brings us to Victor Zsasz, who Stan seems to be playing. There was some speculation when he shaved his head upon joining the production he might be playing the character, but the cast looks to confirm the speculation. While the serial killer—who carves tally marks into his body for every person he’s killed—shows up in Batman Begins as a minor enforcer in Carmine Falcone’s crew, he’s got a much larger role in the comic books themselves. In Long Halloween, Zsasz is hired by Falcone to assassinate Dent before he's intercepted by Batman. Might Reeves look to flip the script here and disfigure Henry’s Dent in the process? This interpretation of Zsasz would certainly fit the extremely grounded approach Reeves took in the first installment. But there’s also some confusion here, as Stan was rumored to be playing Harvey when casting first broke and even went so far as to say he’d be playing the role in an interview over the summer. The French publication Le Journal du Dimanche did, however, later retract his statement.

The last accidental spoiler is a big scoop for comic book fans. Simply labeled “Owl 3,” this likely confirms that the Court of Owls will finally make their silver-screen debut. Created in 2012 by writer Scott Snyder and artist Greg Capullo, the Owls are one of the biggest new additions to the Batman canon in recent memory. The Court is a clandestine criminal society made up of Gotham’s wealthiest and most influential citizens, whose power and influence stretch back to the city’s earliest days. They have immeasurable resources and frequently deploy assassins, known as Talons, to do their bidding. This tracks with the story Reeves told in The Batman of a Gotham beset by a history of corruption. Owls are also bats' natural predators; so that, too, is bad news for Battinson.

While this potential leak is exciting and unexpected, it also raises doubts about the identity of Scarlett Johansson’s character, as she was rumored to be playing Harvey’s wife, Gilda Dent. Either way, never in a million lifetimes could we have guessed that Heidi Klum would be the one to spill the beans about one of the most anticipated comic book movies of the next few years.

#6730. Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

#6729. Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet

While you might think of instant stuffing as a once-a-year darling that makes an annual appearance like Punxsutawney Phil, this recipe is a case study of why this product should be put to use throughout the year. (Boxes of the dried mix can be found near the breadcrumbs any month.) Here, it’s called into action to prop up skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs in a bed of savory stuffing that’s bolstered by aromatics and sweet-tart dried cranberries. Starting with a cold pan ensures even rendering of the chicken fat and crispy skin. The lot gets baked together, allowing the savory drippings from the chicken to soak into the stuffing. Serve with a side of cranberry sauce, a fresh salad, or all by itself for a one-pan dinner that recalls Thanksgiving any night of the week.

More delicious skillet dinners this way: Chicken Thighs With Spiced Couscous and Carrots; Ruffled Mushroom Pot Pie; and One-Skillet Chicken Pot Pie.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Season 2 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (about 4 medium) on both sides with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Pour 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil into a cold large stainless-steel skillet and swirl to coat bottom of pan. Arrange chicken, skin side down, in pan and place over medium-high heat. Cook undisturbed, rotating pan around on burner often to promote even browning, until skin is browned and chicken releases easily from pan, 7–10 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet or large plate and arrange skin side up.

Combine 1 large onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan and cook over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onion is softened and just starting to turn golden, 8–12 minutes. Add one 6-oz. box instant stuffing mix, ½ cup unsweetened dried cranberries, and 1¼ cups water, then finely grate in zest from 1 lemon and set lemon aside. Mix until stuffing is hydrated. Remove pan from heat and push stuffing to sides to create wells for chicken to rest in. Nestle thighs, skin side up, into stuffing. Transfer pan to oven and bake until chicken is cooked through and top of stuffing is golden brown and crisp, 45–55 minutes.

Top chicken and stuffing with more dried cranberries and reserved celery leaves. Cut reserved lemon into wedges and serve alongside for squeezing over.

#6727. The Specific Pain of Outgrowing an Adult Friendship

For my 30th birthday, I hosted a game show about me. It was a ridiculous affair held in West London, where people that I’ve known and loved through the years participated in a series of rounds including: a rap round where guests had to write and perform a verse over Skepta and JME’s “That’s Not Me”; an arts and crafts round where the best drawing of me won; a music round featuring songs from the year I was born; and, of course, a “defend your embarrassing boyfriend” round. The lead-up to 30 was stressful in a way I can’t help but cringe at now; the age carries a symbolic weight that I had attached the pressure of completeness to, as if I’d be cemented at 30 and never change. Despite these irrational fears, my 30th was probably the best celebration I’d ever thrown. After years of dragging friends through intense physical activities—zip-lining, gymnastics, pole, and even aerial skills—a game show felt like a lighter option, something everyone could enjoy.

Still, between the singing, dancing, and early morning revelry, a low hum of sadness accompanied me. There was something missing. It wasn’t that I didn’t appreciate the friends and family who’d come to take part in yet another of my mad ideas; I just felt haunted by the absence of the friends whom I’d assumed would see the day with me. Friends I used to speak to daily—sharing everything from the mundane details of what I had for breakfast to the intricacies of my menstrual cycle—weren’t there for a milestone celebration. It would be easy to say that these friendships had tumultuous endings with clean breaks, where the lines of right and wrong were clearly drawn, but they weren’t, which made it even more painful.

The specific experience of grieving a friendship break-up that cannot be located in a single event is a form of “frozen grief,” a term coined by psychologist Pauline Boss. You are frozen when you cannot process such a loss because its cause is unclear.

Friendship fallouts are an endless source of fuel for the content factory. Women and girls applying makeup or skincare while revealing the story of a best friend who betrayed them can temporarily break the doomscroll. The storyteller is always the victim, the former “best friend” always the villain, and it falls into an easily digestible narrative even when the poster asks, “Am I the problem here?” I often wonder how the breakdown of years-long, nuanced, and complex friendships can be reduced to short clips that portray ex-friends as cartoonishly evil, stripped of their humanity. That said, I do secretly envy posters like this; they have a story, a timeline they can reliably use to trace the end of a friendship.

What I lacked in clarity consumed me with sadness. Kat Vellos, author of We Should Get Together and founder of community program Platonic Action Lab, describes friendship as blooming from four seeds of connection: proximity, frequency, compatibility, and commitment. When the end of a friendship cannot be traced to a single moment of betrayal, she says, it can often be attributed to the absence of one of these seeds.

In my case, certain friendships have fizzled because groups have splintered and formed friendships with other groups, creating new ecosystems I wasn’t part of. It can be hard to trace where things really ended, but sometimes I can remember the last proper conversation we ever had. My friend Fi and I spoke every day, sometimes multiple times—but during busy periods, this happened much less often. A week prior, we’d scheduled a hangout. Nothing out of the ordinary, just a catch-up. It was a busy week; we hadn’t FaceTimed as normal. I texted her on the day to figure out what we’d be doing. She replied instantly, “Sorry, girl, I didn’t hear from you. I’m out with my other friend tonight.” And that was that. We never usually confirmed ahead of time; I’d assumed our friendship was fluid and existed without that level of admin, especially for arranged plans. Still, we never really spoke again. I messaged her on her birthday, but she didn’t message me on mine, and when we saw each other in person, once, it didn’t feel like “no time had passed.” It felt like I’d lived 40 lives since our last conversation, and things were never the same.

The older I get, the fuzzier the image of me with a partner and kids is in my mind’s eye. I’m unsure if my future will involve being focused on a traditional family unit and because of that, my friendships are of utmost importance to me. Friends are not consolation prizes for romantic relationships; they are equally significant, if not even more so. The loss of a friendship feels like the loss of an imagined future we shared. It is the loss of a support system, and it feels even worse when there is no big lesson to be learned from it, no great “wrong” to work through—just an unsatisfying understanding that things change, and sometimes it is beyond our control to stop them.

Though I felt sad at points on my birthday, I was also grateful for all the new relationships that spawned in the wake of old ones; new rituals created and memories shared. There was also something to learn in the grief, as Elizabeth Day writes in Friendaholic: “Perhaps in the letting go, we had understood something integral about ourselves. Perhaps that was all right. Perhaps that was a kind of love.”

#6726. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6723. Chicken Pozole Verde

This chicken pozole verde recipe puts a whole bird to work, making a fragrant broth and plenty of tender shredded meat in one go. Roasted tomatillos and a mix of green chiles give the Mexican stew its tang and heat; a final swirl of cilantro purée adds fresh flavor and turns the whole pot brilliantly green.

The tomatillos and peppers roast while the chicken simmers. Toasting the canned hominy—a tip from Test Kitchen alum Rick Martinez—gives it a flavor “almost like a corn nut.” But if that’s one step too many, skip it—the stew will still be awesome.

Set out red onion, cilantro, dried oregano, and lime wedges, and let everyone load up their own bowl. Add avocado for creaminess, or shredded cabbage, sliced radishes, and crushed tortilla chips for crunch.

Canned white or golden hominy works here. These plump, chewy corn kernels give the stew its hearty texture. Dried hominy needs to be cooked separately before adding it to the pot.

Mexican oregano is a different herb from Mediterranean oregano, with floral, citrusy notes and a hint of anise. We prefer it in this pozole, but regular dried oregano works too.

No. The whole chicken simmers in water with onion, garlic, and spices to make the broth. Before adding the shredded chicken and cilantro purée, taste the broth and season with salt and pepper.

Can I make pozole verde ahead or freeze it?

Yes. Cook the chicken up to 3 days ahead and refrigerate it in its broth, then finish the recipe when you’re ready to serve. You can also freeze the finished pozole. Take Rick’s advice and stash a quart for your next weeknight dinner emergency.

Heat ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Cook 1 large yellow onion, finely chopped, and 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, seasoning with kosher salt and stirring occasionally, until very tender, 12–15 minutes. Add 2 tsp. ground coriander, 1 tsp. ground cumin, and ½ tsp. dried oregano, preferably Mexican, and cook, stirring constantly, until very fragrant, about 1 minute.

Place one 3½–4-lb. whole chicken in pot and pour in 12 cups water. Bring to a simmer and cook chicken, uncovered and reducing heat as needed to maintain a very gentle simmer (and turning once or twice if it isn’t completely submerged), until cooked through and legs wiggle easily in their joints, 40–50 minutes.

Meanwhile, preheat oven to 425°. Spread out 4 poblano chiles, 2 Cubanelle peppers or 2 more poblano chiles, 3 serrano chiles, and 1½ lb. tomatillos, husks removed, rinsed, on a large rimmed baking sheet. Roast, tossing once or twice, until chiles and peppers are browned and collapsing and tomatillos are tender, 30–40 minutes. Let cool.

Transfer chicken to a cutting board; set broth in pot aside. Let chicken sit until cool enough to handle. Pull meat from bones and shred into bite-size pieces; discard chicken skin and bones.

Split open chiles and peppers; remove stems and seeds and discard. Remove any skin that can be easily peeled off and discard. Transfer chiles and peppers to a blender and add tomatillos; reserve baking sheet. Blend until smooth. Stir chile purée into reserved broth and bring to a simmer. Reserve blender.

Spread out two 15-oz. cans golden or white hominy, rinsed, in an even layer on reserved baking sheet and roast, tossing halfway through, until very fragrant and hominy around edges of baking sheet are just beginning to brown, 12–18 minutes. Scrape into pot with broth.

Season broth with salt and freshly ground black pepper and simmer, uncovered, until flavors come together and broth is rich tasting, about 20 minutes. Ladle ½ cup broth into reserved blender. Add 2 cups cilantro leaves with tender stems and purée until smooth and very bright green, at least 1 minute. Add chicken to broth and cook until heated through, then stir in cilantro purée. Taste posole and season with more salt if needed.

Divide posole among bowls. Top with ½ small red onion, thinly sliced, and more cilantro leaves and dried oregano. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing over.

Do Ahead: Chicken can be cooked 3 days ahead. Let cool in broth; cover and chill.

#6722. The Clarks Wallabee Goes Gorpcore

Clarks has been on one lately. Over the past few weeks, Moncler worked up the British footwear brand's signature Wallabee, while A.P.C. took on the Desert Boot and the Weaver. Now, Clarks has called in Italian shoemaker Diemme to drag three of its biggest silhouettes up a mountain.

(In case you don't spend all day thinking about Italian hiking boots, here's a primer: Diemme was founded in Montebelluna, a town in northern Italy with a very serious footwear-making history. The brand is best known for taking the kinda boots originally built for mountains and making them nice enough to wear with your very best trousers. Every pair is still made at its factory in Veneto, and the upcoming Clarks collection is, too.)

The main event is the Wallabee, of course. Diemme reworked the familiar moccasin-shaped shoe and covered it in pale “champagne” suede from Charles F. Stead, the British tannery responsible for some of the nicest fuzzy leather in footwear. So far, so classic. But then you get the thick rope laces and rubber mudguard wrapped around the bottom. Underneath, the OG crepe sole has been swapped out for the chunky, lugged unit found on Diemme's Roccia Vet and Cornaro boots. It makes the whole shoe sit higher and gives it enough tread to deal with more than a slightly sticky pub floor. Your ’Bees are now ready to hit the trails.

There are two more styles in the cross-branded collection. The Desert Boot comes in the classic “cola” brown suede, only now it's been fitted with a heavy-duty sole. Then there's the Desert Trek, which has been transformed into a mid-cut boot and made from black full-grain leather. It keeps the signature center seam and little Trek Man logo, but it's easily the biggest and baddest of the three, with metal D-rings running up the lacing system and a beefed up ankle for extra support.

The Diemme x Clarks collection is set to drop on November 5, purchasable through Diemme, Clarks, and select stockists globally.

A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

#6721. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6720. What to Read, Watch, and Listen to According to the Spring 2027 Collections

Our extensive analyses of the spring 2027 season now contine into the broader realm of culture. This, on the heels of decoding the trends—both what to where and how, clocking the art influences, and highlighting trenchant quotes from the reviews.

One way to fill in the six-month lag between the close of the season and the arrival of clothes in stores is to go deeper into designers’ inspirations. The list below collects the books, movies, and tracks that inspired the spring 2027 collections.

The French philosopher Michel Foucault, the Bloomsbury writer Virginia Woolf, and the photographer Bettina Rheims all make more than one appearance here, as does Baz Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet, a perennial fashion fave. You might want to take a listen to the 1972 Italian song written in gibberish that was the soundtrack to Fendi’s show or rewatch the romantic idyll that is Merchant Ivory’s 1985 film A Room With a View (based on E. M. Forester’s novel), which was Simone Rocha’s touchstone for the men’s collection she presented at Pitti Uomo. And how fitting that Valentino’s show, presented in a library, should include a sheer tulle pullover, the equivalent of a glossy book cover. Alessandro Michele had been ruminating on a concept put forth in the book Black Swan.

“The astounding Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève played host to Alessandro Michele’s latest Valentino show. For the occasion, Michele produced a sort of bibliography of imagined books, complete with descriptions, made-up authors, and phony ISBNs. Among the many creative titles were A Garden of Small Errors, Elsewhere Is a Precise Place, and The Social Life of Velvet. In the copious show notes, he talked up the value of an ‘anti-library’ of unread books (a concept lifted from the Lebanese American scholar Nassim Nicholas Taleb), comparing the enormous potential such a trove contains to a closetful of unworn clothes.

‘Even the garments that we will never wear, no differently than those books sitting unopened on our shelves, still speak to us of the lives we could have lived. Not as regrets, but as promises,’ Michele wrote.”—Nicole Phelps

“ ‘I read that book called Foucault in California,’ Tron said before the show. ‘It’s about him experimenting with LSD in Death Valley, and basically this idea of the desert as a space for expanding consciousness, experimenting, also disillusion.’ From there, he said, came ‘American desert psychedelicism, Jim Morrison, sexuality, Joan Didion, Walter De Maria’—a collision between the strictures of French intellectual thought and the psychic expansiveness of the American West.”—Luke Leitch

“…Pay Per View, a collection about the slippery, sensual business of being watched—and what happens to the self when we know there is an audience. Zinko had been reading Michel Foucault on Jeremy Bentham’s panopticon: the circular prison structure in which inmates cannot know at any given moment whether the guard at its center is observing them, and therefore start to regulate their own behavior. ‘Modern society revolves around live-streaming and social media, and it forces us to behave as if we are constantly being perceived,’ she said.”—Anna Cafolla

“She had been reading Women Who Run with the Wolves, Clarissa Pinkola Estés’s 1992 bestseller about reconnecting with an instinctual female power. In Ahn’s home of Tokyo, the tension between the expectations of society and the pull of nature is palpable: ‘Japanese people are really in their heads, especially in the city, because there are so many unwritten rules we need to follow. Because of that, the city is like a well-oiled machine, and everything is functioning, but when you’re in it, I feel like it drives all that energy up to your head.’ ”—Ashley Ogawa Clarke

“For her spring 2027 collection, ‘Lost to Virtue,’ Laura Gerte explored the deconstruction of femininity’s moral ideals. Her starting point was research into Dadaism and the work of artist and poet Mina Loy, whose feminist manifesto, written in 1914, framed female ‘virtue’—or rather virginity—as a patriarchal tool of control. Published only decades later, the text still felt radical enough to hint at just how provocative it must have been in its own time.

‘One of the manifesto’s central ideas is the destruction of virtue. For generations, the idea of female morality has been used to keep girls and women small, forcing us into predefined roles. And we don’t want that anymore,’ Gerte said after the show.”—Valerie Specht

“Dushane Noble is tapped into the ongoing discourse around taste as a social signifier. Can taste be acquired like wealth or commodities? (Tech bros sure think so.) Is it just something else to be flattened by the algorithm?

Status and Culture: How Our Desire For Social Rank Creates Taste, Identity, Art, Fashion And Constant Change by W. David Marx informed Noble’s spring 2027 collection. ‘[Marx] talks about this idea of status-seeking being the quiet engine behind taste and culture—that what we see as cool or good taste is really status,’ Noble explained.”—Hannah Jackson

“The designer built her spring 2027 collection around Florian Illies’ book, 1913: The Year Before the Storm. ‘It was about how all the European artists and thinkers and scientists at that moment were living their life as if there was no tomorrow,’ the designer explained. ‘There was really this sense of creativity and how they were working together that was really inspiring to me; there was something that felt so parallel to the time that we live in today.’ ”—Laird Borrelli-Persson

“For their [10th] anniversary collection, the duo drew inspiration from the recently published book Modestadt Berlin by historian Gesa Kessemeier; through years of research, she documented the flourishing fashion scene of pre-war Berlin and highlighted long-forgotten names such as Joe Strassner, Johanna Marbach, and Uli Richter.”—Kerstin Weng

“ ‘If you know me, you know that I'm obsessed with a thing that’s just for a thing,’ said Daniella Kallmeyer. That ‘thing’ this season was a book about traditional Japanese packaging titled How to Wrap Five Eggs. The cover art, which features eggs gently crocheted together, became a bit of an obsession for its structural discipline and textural intrigue. It captures when an obsession becomes a meditative practice, and in the Kallmeyer world, that inevitably becomes a collection. (Sharp eyes hopefully caught the bright flash of eggs nestled in their crochet carrier swinging against a trench-length blouson-bottomed coat.)”—Alexandra Hildreth

“His latest he dubbed ‘Remnants and Relics,’ and very good it was too; a time-traveling 400-year odyssey with an Orlando-type character who gathers up a wardrobe of ivory high-buttoned, foppish suiting with a Death in Venice vibe to it. … ‘The collection is based on the Virginia Woolf character,’ Mario Keine said after his show, ‘but it’s also a development of last season’s, which was based on the Enlightenment [the 18th century movement where fearful superstition gave way to rational, empirical knowledge]. Today we’re also looking for knowledge, even though we’re meant to have it all because it’s on our phones.’ ”—Mark Holgate

“Home as a shelter was the genesis of Marco Rambaldi’s spring 2027 collection. From a reference to Virginia Woolf’s A Room of One’s Own, the Bolognese designer developed the concept of a space where anyone who enters can express themselves freely, without any judgment.”—Alberto Calabrese

“ ‘One can do without meat, but cannot live where there is no bamboo; lacking meat merely leads to weight loss, whereas lacking bamboo means losing peace of mind.’ This poem by the Song dynasty scholar Su Shi became a guiding reference for this knockout IM Men collection, which was all about bamboo.”—Ashley Ogawa Clarke

“This season he’s been thinking about The Little Mermaid, and related with the metaphor of looking up towards the surface. This wasn’t a Disneyfied ‘Part of Your World’ expression, but one that in typical Yusho fashion drew on the original story’s darker themes: the pain of walking on one’s feet in an unfamiliar world, the realization that the sea water running down the mermaid’s cheeks was really tears, and maybe the hint of regret at making a choice that can no longer be reversed.”—Ashley Ogawa Clarke

“Many models wore floppy white cloche hats, which Murakami said referenced Shiroi Boshi (The White Hat), a Japanese children’s story. The premise is too convoluted to summarize here, but the point Murakami was making was one of beauty in abstraction. ‘It’s about dissolving the boundaries between the real world and fantasy,’ he said. ‘That’s how I view memory, after all. We might casually look at things like the sky, or a coat hanger’—he gestured to one in the room—‘but the images we’ve built up in our minds are often slightly twisted or blurred at the edges. I feel there’s immense value in being able to sense and appreciate those kinds of nuances.’ ”—Ashley Ogawa Clarke

The “collection was entitled Skin and based around the idea of an outer surface continually shed, renewed, and rewritten, with the phoenix, specifically Osamu Tezuka’s Phoenix, providing the central image of rebirth.”—Luke Leitch

“She started, she said, from her reading the play The Bitter Tears of Petra von Kant. It’s a reference, with its woman fashion designer as a central character that has inspired many for years; yet Dujancourt took it in her own way. Drawing on her experience of synesthesia, the visual suggestion of the title triggered her to create a ‘tears library’—strings of lace and crochet, representing ‘despair, grief, pain, and relief.’ ”—Sarah Mower

“Susan Fang has been in the midst of designing costumes for M. Butterfly, an opera by Huang Ruo showing at the La Monnaie / De Munt in Brussels next year. … Naturally, the plot of M. Butterfly has been top of mind for Fang. Though rather than lifting references directly from the story to inform her spring collection, she looked to holistic moods and feelings. Specifically, the ‘imagined worlds people create around love,’ as she explained at a preview.”—Alice Cary

“The invitation was a wedding announcement: that of Ippolita and Antiogu, in Alghero, ‘the midday after St. John’s night.’ …the collection’s title hid another layer: ‘A Midsummer Midday Wedding’ nodded to Shakespeare, whose midsummer comedy ends with the wedding of Theseus and Hippolyta, Ippolita in Italian, while Antiogu is the Sardinian form of Antioco.”—Giorgia Feroldi

“Casa Susanna, a photo book chronicling the lives and loves of a group of mid-century men who dressed as women at a country retreat in the Catskills Mountains, was Joseph Altuzarra’s starting point for spring. Something about Susanna Valenti and her friends’ expressiveness served as an unlock for Altuzarra. ‘I just love how joyful it was,’ he said. ‘I really wanted the collection to feel joyful, to be all about color and this idea of freedom.’ ”—Nicole Phelps

“Isabel Marant is the quintessential Parisian brand, but for spring creative director Kim Bekker found her inspiration a world away, in LA. There, she came across a ’60s book of photographs by Sam Haskins showing women bathed in hazy light, dressed or undressed. ‘The colors were almost translucent,’ Bekker said.”—Tina Isaac-Goizé

“ ‘I started from a very simple idea—to continue exploring an Italian way of life defined by authenticity, quality, and a natural relationship with objects,’ Matteo Tamburini said. …Simplicity, however, is seldom simple. Tamburini’s point of departure was Viaggio in Italia, Luigi Ghirri’s seminal 1984 photographic project, which offered a new way of seeing the country: attentive rather than sentimental, curious and slightly raw rather than steeped in clichés.”—Tiziana Cardini

“Inspired by Modern Lovers (1990), photographer Bettina Rheims’s portrait series exploring the performance and plurality of gender identities, Yanagawa subtly disrupted his signature tailoring—blazers and suits cut long or cropped—with conventionally feminine gestures: lace peeking from sleeves, mesh tulle, crushed velvet, glossy patent finishes, and shorts designed to resemble skirts. Altercasting completed the picture with models that looked lifted straight from Rheims’s photographs, slicked-back hair included.”—Valerie Specht

Charlotte Knowles and Alexandre Arsenault “will be celebrating their brand’s 10th anniversary next year, and found themselves returning to a central source of inspiration for their graduate show at Central Saint Martins: the French photographer Bettina Rheims’s landmark book Chambre Close, which featured images of women undressing across a series of cheap, anonymous hotel rooms. ‘We’ve been feeling nostalgic about where we started, and we thought it would be an interesting exercise to think about how we see things now, versus how we saw them back then,’ Arsenault said at a preview. Added Knowles: ‘All the women in the book are in different stages of undress, so we translated that into the collection quite literally: a lot of deconstruction and layering. We also took inspiration from the colors and went a little more zingy with the palette. It’s really about our twist on femininity.’ ”—Liam Hess

“ ‘I always try to go with a little bit of romance and beauty, but I always try to give it this grunge element,’ Hillary Taymour said at a preview. The designer carried over some 18th-century loveliness (see the opening ruffled moiré cape) from the not-for-sale collection she presented at Copenhagen Fashion Week and introduced medieval (see the plaid printed sequined fabric that is a stand-in for chain mail) after watching Heath Ledger and Shannyn Sossamon in A Knight’s Tale on the flight back. ‘My whole goal is to make everything big and voluminous and as light as possible,’ said Taymour.”—Laird Borrelli-Persson

“For spring 2027, his 11th season, he felt the urge to connect back to the brand’s foundations, in part as a response to his father’s recent passing. ‘There’s a more somber tone,’ he said. Miles Davis and Tupac served as touchstones, as did the movie Ichi the Killer and the Japanese actor Takeshi Kitano.”—Max Berlinger

“Wong Kar-wai’s In The Mood For Love was the starting point for Patrick McDowell’s spring 27 collection titled Love. It’s also the designer’s partner’s favorite film. In it actress Maggie Cheung wears 21 cheongsams of different prints …. It was one of those prints McDowell translated into the green stripe silk material that was the protagonist of today's show, taking inspiration from the film’s dominant hues of red and green.”—Electra Kostoni

“There was a whiff of the 1980s, she said, in the Hawaiian shirts (the print based on the one Leonardo DiCaprio wears in Baz Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet and a picture of Bruce Willis), and cropped, garment-dyed, coated-nylon cargo jackets in Miami Vice hues.”—Max Berlinger

“Dsquared2’s Dean and Dan Caten went deeper into Italian-ness for their spring 2027. In fact, the duo drew on the Mediterranean folklore of southern Italy, exploring religious symbolism through a spicy lens. Crosses and holy references, along with religious-inspired tattoos, were at the core of this season, with nods to Baz Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet.

This was especially evident in the gangster-inspired atmosphere, a choice that showcased Dsquared2’s propensity to mix up very different references, often rooted in pop culture.”—Alberto Calabrese

“The starting point was Green Snake, Tsui Hark’s 1993 film starring Maggie Cheung and Joey Wong, a modern retelling of the ancient Chinese legend of the white snake. For designers Samuel Yang and Erik Litzén, the duo behind the label, there was no shortage of material to shed and reassemble.”—Tiziana Cardini

“While gestating the collection, Rocha returned to the 1985 Merchant Ivory movie adaptation of Forster’s book, reacquainting herself with an Oscar-winning suite of Edwardian costume design by Jenny Beavan and John Bright almost as exquisitely realized as Florence itself. ‘This is my Irish man and he’s arrived in Florence and become the main character,’ she said of a designed ensemble that was inhabited by multiple character studies.”—Luke Leitch

“Opening with sharp tailoring and an elegant Dalmatian print on skirts and blouses, it read like something Cruella de Vil would have worn had she been a Wall Street big shot in the ’80s.

Instead, it was the much cooler 1982 cult-classic Smithereens that Reid Baker and Inês Amorim were inspired by, which also informed the bold punky checks that were mixed in, all finished off with leather driving gloves and wraparound statement sunglasses that lent a sleek edge.”—Ashley Ogawa Clarke

“ ‘I always tell the Los Angeles story, the rock and roll, something sunny and optimistic,’ Amiri said backstage. ‘But one night I watched American Gigolo, and I saw Los Angeles in a very dark way, a seductive way.’ From there, he was sketching out a script involving a cast of sharp-dressed night crawlers, thinking about where they’d be glimpsed in the shadows of dimly lit bars or the back rooms of private members’ clubs. ‘There’s something dangerous about these characters and the places they go.’ ”—Sarah Mower

“As the designer acknowledged, it’s ‘kind of strange’ for Ann Demeulemeester to take inspiration from L.A. But he said he’s fascinated by the darker side of the city. During his trip, Gallici watched Billy Wilder’s 1950 dark comedy Sunset Boulevard and started to see Los Angeles through a more sinister lens. ‘I was thinking about how L.A. is the ghost of a city that once was so florid. It’s almost a city worn to death,’ he said.”—Lucy Maguire

“As they were building out the theme, the pair watched any number of movies relating to Hollywood—Sunset Boulevard, Boogie Nights, Hollywood 90028, All That Jazz, They Shoot Horses, Don’t They?, Cabaret. The last is especially up August Barron’s alley; the designers are interested in the elusiveness or the decay of fame, the wearing away of its gold plating.”—Laird Borrelli-Persson

“Yuka Kimura called this Mukcyen collection Low Energy. The designer, who is on her sixth season of the brand, had been watching Michelangelo Antonioni’s 1964 film Red Desert, which explores the psychological toll of industrialization, and was thinking about how it relates to our present reality.

Nowadays the grind of factories and machinery has been replaced by a ceaseless hum of digital noise. ‘A messy, overwhelming variety of inputs,’ as Kimura put it. ‘People are becoming increasingly sensitive to this kind of noise, or simply exhausted by it,’ she said. ‘I created this collection to express that feeling.’ ”—Ashley Ogawa Clarke

“Romance, ERD-style, has a dark undertow: the show notes evoked ‘a mysterious unnamed figure who destabilizes a wealthy bourgeois family by seducing every member of the household.’ Pasolini fans will recognize the late, great Terence Stamp in Teorema. There’s always a hint of trouble brewing.”—Tina Isaac-Goizé

“Leandro Cano is frustrated by how often Andalusia is underestimated. That frustration became the starting point for Le Chien Andalou, his latest collection. …

Religion and flamenco traditions became two of the collection’s foundations, filtered through the same surrealist lens as Luis Buñuel’s famous film, which gave the collection its name. ‘This time I’m working from three ideas: hyperbole, beauty, and surrealism, which I accept as something completely natural,’ said Cano.”—Nuria Lui

“Francesco Murano went to Metropolis for his starting point (a particularly timely choice, given that Fritz Lang’s 1927 vision is set in 2026), and to the film’s two Marias for his central dichotomy: the virtuous woman and her seductive robotic double.

His response, a collection called Éidola, which is Ancient Greek for ‘image,’ took the two and, sensibly, refused to choose.”—Tiziana Cardini

“Biga landed on Theodore Dryer’s black-and-white 1928 film, The Passion of Joan of Arc, as his spring inspiration. This martyr might be fashion’s favorite saint, and pop culture likes her too: Hlynur Pálmason released his own Joan of Arc film last year, and Baz Luhrmann is developing one as well. Biga was drawn to the he/she aspects of this historical figure who refused to give up her faith—and the menswear she wore.”—Laird Borrelli-Persson

“The show melted two stories together, those of A Bug’s Life and the fairytale of the princess and the frog: except ‘in this case it’s the prince and the frog,’ Browne said.”—Luke Leitch

“The designer explained that he had three points of departure: Studio Ghibli’s The Secret World of Arrietty; the Sylvanian Families he has been collecting with his young relatives (those inspired the tactile velvets, wide-wale corduroys and lamés) and Alice’s mushroom-eating adventures in the Wonderland. But he leavened the vibe with pointed commentary. ‘I figured since the world is so fucked up right now, we might as well turn everything upside down,’ Ortuño Perez quipped.”—Tina Isaac-Goizé

“For spring 2027, designer Louis-Gabriel Nouchi looked to America’s Pacific Northwest, specifically the David Lynch version as depicted in his cult-classic TV show, Twin Peaks. That not only gave the collection its desired outdoorsy feel (those Boy Scout shorts and ranger shirts!) but provided a cast of archetypes (the detective, the cop, the endangered ingenue) and a creeping sense of darkness, of strangeness. Add to that the navy/gray/brown/purple palette of Francis Bacon and a touch of Blade Runner’s dystopian futurism, and the broad contours of his collection started to coalesce accordingly.”—Max Berlinger

“ ‘[Golden Girls] was not actually the inspiration for the collection, but in hindsight we realized that it has a lot to do with it and there are elements that feel very Golden Girls,’ added Lazo. ‘I would say 90% of that series is the women in their dressing gowns or bathrobes eating cheesecake, and that also became a talking point in the collection.’

“ ‘We put a beefcake in the cheesecake,’ ”Schmidl quipped.”—Laird Borrelli-Persson

“In 1972 the Milanese musician Adriano Celentano conducted an experiment: He released a song without meaning, its lyrics written entirely in gibberish meant to sound like English, to see if it could still move an audience. At first the song bombed. But two nationally televised performances featuring group choreography and Celentano’s own distinctive dancing—his nickname was Il Molleggiato, or ‘The Bouncy’—saw it rise high in the charts, first in Italy and then in multiple countries across Europe. …

One of those two TV performances featured another Italian pop progressive, Raffaella Carrà, whose immortal Italo-disco banger ‘Rumore’ was mixed into the ‘Prisencolinensinainciusol’-dominated soundtrack at Maria Grazia Chiuri’s Fendi show today. You could see Celentano’s experimental approach in 1972 as a mirror of Chiuri’s in 2026. Speaking at a preview, she said: “ ‘Fashion is part of our language.… Clothes give another sense to the body.’ She added: ‘Fashion is that. What do you like? What is your memory? Putting this together is like being a DJ. I think it is impossible to concentrate on only one aspect.’ ”—Luke Leitch

True Blue, presented by the Brodie Sessions, as the Skovgaardettes, from left: Lauren Glading, Sharleen Chidiac, and Maya Laner.

“Skovgaard, who grew up with the Spice Girls (and identified with Baby Spice) was turned onto The Supremes, The Ronettes, and The Shangri-las while watching a Danish television series about the ’60s. He started researching them, ‘but instead of just reusing the vibe of those three girl groups, I wanted to create a fictional girl group instead because I couldn’t really see [the others] representing the collection I was dreaming of making,’ he explained. So ‘I decided to come up with this imaginary girl group called the Skovgaardettes.’ ”—Laird Borrelli-Persson

“The show had two phases, each delineated by music: Chaka Khan’s ‘Like Sugar’

and Michael Jackson’s ‘I Just Can’t Stop Loving You.’ ”—Luke Leitch

“It looks like goodbye at Saint Laurent. Ten years and precisely two days since his 2016 debut, Anthony Vaccarello took his last bow at the Kering-owned brand. At least, the signs pointed that way.

The music playing as guests filtered in was Miles Davis’s soundtrack to Louis Malle’s first film, the meaningfully named Elevator to the Gallows.”—Nicole Phelps

“The collection began with an assortment of images by photographer Trevor Hughes, whose bike-messenger series in 1990s Toronto captured an innate understanding of styling. Partly born from athletic and functional necessity, and partly from pure inherent fashion, such as a zip-up minidress styled over bike shorts, Hughes’s messengers captured what so many are trying to chase, becoming the basis for Attersee’s spring collection.”—Alexandra Hildreth

“ ‘I wanted to explore falling in all its forms,’ Kegels said. The runway included portions of stretch fabric, suspended just above the ground, to show the weight of each step. (It was inspired by a YouTube video of science educator Dan Burns, who used a similar setup to explain Einstein’s theory of general relativity.)”—Lucy Maguire

#6718. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6717. A '90s Prada Obsessive Picks Her Four Favorite Collections

To know Laia Garcia-Furtado is to understand that she’s obsessed with Prada. Indeed, it’s one of her most obvious traits. During her tenure as senior fashion news editor here at Vogue, she spoke at length about her expertise on Miuccia Prada on our podcast, “The Run-Through,” and wrote countless odes to her beloved brand. So when she was approached by an editor at Batsford Books with a proposal to write a book on Prada, it felt preordained. “I feel like I’ve been training my entire life for this,” she said. Still, as an editor herself, Garcia-Furtado had to gut-check herself. “I quickly remembered that there’s a lot more to ’90s Prada than those legendary collections that came in the second half of the decade.”

Her new book Prada in the Nineties comes at a great time for the new generation of Miuccia-heads, discovering the brand on social media. “I think everyone is still so obsessed with the ’90s because, looking back, we think of it as the last decade of a kind of freedom,” Garcia-Furtado explains. “The Internet was barely beginning, and people still dressed to their own spirit. But I think for Prada, especially, this is the decade where it went from a kind of fledgling label to the global behemoth it is today.” She adds that it was during this period that Mrs. Prada discovered her voice and encompassing vision for what the brand would one day become. “All those ’90s collections are still constantly referenced to this day.”

Even as a devotee, the research process yielded a treasure trove of information about Mrs. Prada, like the fact that the designer’s spring 1999 collection was actually her way of fighting back against the trends of the ’90s (trends, of course, she helped popularize). “The spring 1999 collection with mirror embellishments was her sort of ‘taking the piss’ to the hippie trend that was happening around the time,” says Garcia-Furtado. “I love when you see her humor peeking through, and that really reminded me of the lace collection from fall 2008—another one of my all-time favorites—that she said she made because she hated lace.”

Because the book is unauthorized and unapproved by Prada—as she wittily notes on her cover—Garcia-Furtado tapped illustrator Rachel Song to reimagine her favorite collections (think a chinoiserie look on page 133 or the spring 1999 bumbag on page 167). When asked if she’s sent a copy to Prada headquarters yet, she had a pithy reply: “You can’t just reach out to God like that.” Here’s to hoping a copy makes its way to Milan regardless.

On the occasion of the book being published, we asked Garcia-Furtado to share her four favorite ’90s Prada collections, and explain what makes them so special.

“I think spring 1994 is maybe an underrated collection, or maybe it was underrated to me, and now I love it. The strange sheer nightgowns layered over knitted separates and worn with little white socks and odd moccasins. The sudden Renaissance influence with the leather vests over the dreamy white dresses. It really captured the grunge spirit of the time yet in a purely Miuccia way, but I think it’s still really modern.”

“Spring 1996 is maybe my all-time favorite fashion collection, the root cause of my personal style. The mismatched prints, all the different shades of green that are supposed to be ugly but couldn’t possibly be. (It’s worth noting that my teen girl bedroom had two walls painted bright slime green and two opposing walls painted mint green—so I wouldn’t go totally crazy according to my mom.) But even beyond the prints, the silhouettes are pure Prada: a midi-length skirt ending in the no man’s land between knee and ankle, a simple slip dress worn under a car coat, strange sandals that expose entirely too much toe. Everything feels a little bit off, but it’s also perfectly feminine, perfectly balanced.”

“This was the season when Mrs. Prada started thinking about the future, like suddenly the idea of the new millennium became real. Everything looks a little bit tech-y yet also romantic, as if it came from a near-distant past. Beads look like the inside of a computer or maybe drops of rain? Her favorite little button-down shirts now come with latex insets. I also love the berry color palette, both in the ladylike suits with oddly-gathered skirts, and on the lips! Also, this season had those divine pink lucite heels that are definitely at the top of my wish list.”

#6716. 23 Thanksgiving Bread Recipes: Rolls, Biscuits, and More

Pies get most of the Thanksgiving baking glory. But these Thanksgiving bread recipes make a strong case for saving some oven space for buttery dinner rolls, flaky biscuits, and midnight-sandwich-ready loaves. Think golden sweet potato buns soft enough to nap on, buttermilk cornbread to eat with butter or bake into dressing, and tender sweet loaves to nibble on Thanksgiving morning. Several recipes have make-ahead options too.

There’s no need to overhaul a classic. Adapted from The Fannie Farmer Baking Book, these Parker House rolls have buttery folds, golden tops, and a finish of flaky salt. Pair them with our classic Thanksgiving menu.

These pillowy rolls get their warm color and gentle sweetness from mashed sweet potato. Bake and freeze them up to a month ahead, then reheat and brush with melted butter before serving.

Butter tucked inside each roll melts as it bakes, crisping the bottom. “If you can imagine a warm dinner roll meeting a flaky croissant, you’re getting closer,” says Hana Asbrink.

Pillowy rolls swirled with sweet-salty pork floss, mayo, scallions, and furikake. Bake and freeze them up to three months ahead, then warm them through while everyone finds a seat.

A tangzhong—a cooked flour-and-milk paste—helps these sour cream and chive rolls stay exceptionally soft. Tear one off to mop up gravy, then save a few for tomorrow’s turkey sandwiches.

Garlic bread, meet buttery dinner roll. Fresh and dried dill work their way into these pillowy buns, which get a generous brushing of garlic butter after baking. Save one for a gravy swipe.

So many layers, you’ll feel like a geologist unearthing them. Claire Saffitz’s biscuits get their height from a cut-and-stack technique. Another reason to love them: You can freeze the unbaked biscuits up to a month ahead.

All the herby goodness of Thanksgiving stuffing, packed into a biscuit: sage, rosemary, fennel seed, and scallions. Save a few for breakfast the next morning, preferably under a generous ladle of leftover gravy.

No rolling pin, no biscuit cutter, no problem. Canned creamed corn keeps these drop biscuits tender, while Calabrian chile honey butter brings a little heat.

For the guest who always takes the biggest piece of garlic bread: flaky buttermilk biscuits loaded with Parmesan and parsley. Freeze them unbaked, then bake straight from frozen when the oven frees up.

Biscuits or cornbread? This cheesy mash-up means you don’t have to choose. Sharp cheddar and fresh sage work their way into flaky, buttery layers that feel right at home on the Thanksgiving table.

Looking to start a fight? Declare a cornbread recipe “best.” This version strikes a balance: a tender crumb, buttermilk tang, and a touch of sweetness. Eat it with butter—or turn it into cornbread dressing.

Cheddar, caramelized corn, and hot honey butter take this cornbread well beyond the usual. Nervous about the flip? “Don’t be afraid of flipping the bread—I promise you can do it,” says former BA food editor Rachel Gurjar.

Pumpkin purée gives this fall-ish rendition of our no-knead focaccia recipe its golden color and gentle sweetness. Finish with rosemary and flaky salt, then tear off a piece for dipping in olive oil. You can bake it a day ahead.

Leave the oven to the turkey. These flaky, skillet-cooked parathas have brown butter and sage tucked between their layers. Parcook them a day ahead, then fry until golden just before dinner.

A garlic knot with centerpiece ambitions. This braided loaf wraps buttery dough around garlic, Parmesan, and parsley, then gets another garlicky brush after baking. Start the dough a day ahead.

Leave the stand mixer where it is. This focaccia asks for a little patience, not much elbow grease, to produce its airy crumb and golden crust. An overnight rise gets you started; garlic butter finishes the job.

Focaccia’s leaf-shaped French cousin deserves a turn in the Thanksgiving bread basket. Green olives, rosemary, and lemon zest bring plenty of flavor. And yes, the dough comes together in one bowl.

In this crusty yeast bread recipe, apple juice replaces water. The apple flavor is subtle, but the appeal of a warm slice with butter is not.

Oats and chia seeds give this gluten-free loaf a dense, chewy crumb. No kneading, shaping, or scoring; just be sure to use the gluten-free oats and oat flour specified in the recipe.

Give Thanksgiving morning the sticky-bun treatment. This pull-apart bread packs tender apples between cinnamon-sugar-coated bites, with tangy cider caramel coating the whole thing. Put on a pot of coffee and let everyone help themselves.

Chocolate or vanilla? Rick Martinez’s conchas give you both, with a two-tone sugar topping over buttery Mexican sweet buns. Another reason to love them: You can bake them up to three days ahead.

Start the holiday with a thick slice of ginger-spiked pumpkin bread and a generous schmear of salted maple butter. You can bake the loaf up to four days ahead, leaving Thanksgiving morning for coffee and slicing—and, uh, all that other prep.

Maple-glazed turkey, garlicky mashed potatoes, pumpkin chiffon pie, and more recipes worthy of your Thanksgiving table.

Like brown-butter brussels sprouts with gochujang, green bean salad with Parmesan dressing, our best-ever mashed potatoes, and more reasons to rebrand the holiday “Sidesgiving.”

From hot toddies to big-batch punch, these festive drinks will get you in the holiday spirit.

#6715. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.
